In build

Archie Mobile.

The app we are building for your phone.

Your agent already reaches you anywhere, through a chat app. This is the version where the messages in between are sealed, and we cannot read them either.

Written and running here, not finished, and in neither app store. Nothing on this page is something you can install today.

Today

Where your agent’s words go now.

Your agent reaches you through a chat app you already use: Telegram, Discord, Slack, Matrix, or iMessage on a Mac. It is the reason you can be anywhere and still be reachable, and it has one consequence worth saying out loud: what your agent tells you crosses that company’s servers, the same as any other message you send there.

That is true of every agent you can reach this way, not just ours, and we would rather you heard it from us. It is also the reason we are building something else.

What it is

Archie on your computer, reachable from your pocket.

Most of what you do at the computer

Start your agent or stop it. Add an add-on or take one off, and finish its setup. Turn a routine on and off, or move the time it runs. Rename it, change its face, read what it has been doing, and talk to it. The things it cannot reach are the things that never leave your computer: your passwords and keys, your knowledge files, the rows inside a collection, and the screenshots a job took.

It is not running your agent

Nothing about your agent moves to your phone. It stays on the computer you installed it on, with your files and your connected accounts, and it keeps working there whether your phone is in your hand, in your pocket, or flat. The app is a way to reach that computer and tell it things, which is also why your computer has to be awake and online for the app to be any use.

The app

Sealed on your computer, before it leaves.

Your computer locks every message before it goes anywhere. The key that opens it is made on your computer, kept in the keychain your operating system already uses for passwords, and handed to your phone by showing a code on the screen for the phone’s camera to read. The key never passes through us.

So we do hold the messages. We just cannot open them. That distinction is the whole claim, and it is the honest form of it: “it never touches our servers” would be punchier and false.

The change is structural, not a setting. With a chat app there is a company in the middle holding your agent’s messages in a form it can open. With the app there is still a company in the middle, and it is us, and we have no key.

This is a second door, not a replacement for the first. Your agent keeps working in the chat app you connected, and most people will want both.

Side by side

Who can open what.

Each chat app Archie connects to, what that company publishes about encryption, and whether that company can open your agent’s messages, compared with the app Otian is building.
  What that company publishes Can they open it
Telegram An ordinary chat, which is the kind an agent uses, is encrypted between your device and Telegram rather than end to end. Telegram’s FAQ says cloud chats are “stored encrypted in the Telegram Cloud”, and that “several court orders from different jurisdictions are required to force us to give up any data”. Its end-to-end kind, a Secret Chat, is between two people on their phones and is not something an agent can useSource 1 Yes
Discord Every voice and video call is end-to-end encrypted, which Discord announced and documents. Text is not covered, in Discord’s own words: “We have no current plans to extend E2EE to text messages”Source 2 Yes
Slack “In Slack, customer data is encrypted at rest and in transit by default.” Archie joins as an ordinary bot in a workspace, so your agent’s messages sit in that workspace like every other message in itSource 3 Yes
Matrix A Matrix room can be end-to-end encrypted. Archie cannot read one that is, so our connect guide asks you to make a room with encryption off. That is the same trade as the others, not a better one, and it is ours rather than Matrix’sSource 4 Yes
iMessage on a Mac The exception, and worth knowing if this is what you care about. Apple encrypts it end to end and says “no one else can access your end-to-end encrypted data, not even Apple”. Archie reads it out of the Messages app on your own computer rather than over the networkSource 5 No
The app we are building Sealed on your computer before it leaves, under a key your computer makes and gives to your phone by camera. We hold the sealed messages and have no key to themSource 6 No, and neither can we
The catch

What sealing does not do.

What we can still see

Three things about each sealed message are not sealed, because something has to read them without a key: when it was left, which version of Archie wrote it, and whether an instruction is waiting, finished or failed. So we can see that a phone is talking to a computer, and roughly when. Never what it said.

Whoever holds the phone holds the key

Sealing protects the message in the middle. It cannot protect you from a phone somebody else is holding, and it never could. The fix is on your computer: unpair that phone, and its key retires with it, so nothing sent afterwards can be opened by it. The same has always been true of the computer itself, where somebody sitting at it unlocked has everything.

Where it stands

Honestly: not finished.

The app is written and it runs. The piece it needs on our side is not switched on yet, and it is in neither app store, so we cannot give you a date and will not invent one. Archie is in testing, and this is part of what testing is for.

Nothing about your setup has to change to be ready for it.

Sources for every claim on this page
1Telegram, on cloud chats and Secret Chats

“Secret chats use end-to-end encryption” while “Cloud Chats use client-server/server-client encryption and are stored encrypted in the Telegram Cloud”, and “several court orders from different jurisdictions are required to force us to give up any data”. From the Telegram FAQ, read on September 11, 2026.

2Discord, on what its encryption covers

Discord’s DAVE protocol covers “every voice and video call on Discord, whether in DMs, group DMs, voice channels, or Go Live streams”, and on text: “We have no current plans to extend E2EE to text messages.” From Discord’s own announcement, read on September 11, 2026.

3Slack, on encryption

“In Slack, customer data is encrypted at rest and in transit by default.” From Slack’s security page, read on September 11, 2026. The second half of that row is about our connection, not about Slack: Archie joins a workspace as an ordinary bot, which you can check in your workspace’s app settings.

4Matrix, and our own limitation

This row is about Archie, not about Matrix. Our Matrix connection cannot read an encrypted room, so the connect guide asks for one with encryption switched off, and the agent says so in the room if it lands in an encrypted one. Matrix supports end-to-end encryption well; the shortfall is ours.

5Apple, on iMessage

“No one else can access your end-to-end encrypted data, not even Apple.” From Apple’s iCloud data security overview, read on September 11, 2026. One caveat Apple states on the same page and we will not leave out: Messages in iCloud is end-to-end encrypted when iCloud Backup is off, so if you keep iCloud Backup on, check how Apple describes that before relying on it.

6Our side of the table

The sealed mailbox already exists and already carries phone access: what we hold, what stays readable and what we cannot open is set out on the Trust page, each line pointing at the code behind it. The app uses that same mailbox. Messages are sealed with AES-256-GCM, an ordinary published cipher rather than anything of our own invention, and the key travels in the part of a web address browsers never send to a server.

What we have not claimed

Nothing here says Telegram, Discord or Slack read your messages. It says what each company publishes about what it can do, and links you to their words so you can check ours. Nothing here says a chat app is unsafe to use: your agent works there today, we built those connections on purpose, and we are not asking anyone to stop. And nothing here claims to be the most secure anything: we have not tested every product that exists, so we have described one mechanism and shown you where it fails.

Next

Reaching your agent already works.

You do not have to wait for this to have your agent in your pocket. Connecting a chat app takes a few minutes and is the last step of setting one up: How It Works walks through it, and now you know what that choice means.

If what you want first is the full list of what we hold while you use it, that is the Trust page, written to be checked rather than believed.
